message.content: {"28": {"original": "DRM is wrong because it actively stops the right to repair, which is a core free", "rephrased": "Digital Rights Management systems are fundamentally flawed because they actively prevent users from repairing the devices they own, thereby violating the essential freedom to study and fix hardware that contains proprietary software. This restriction undermines the core principle of the free software movement, which asserts that users must have the right to access source code and modify the programs running their physical tools. Consequently, any technology or legal framework that locks users out of maintaining or fixing their own property should be rejected in favor of systems that guarantee user control and repairability.", "summary": "Digital Rights Management violates user freedom by preventing device repair and must be eliminated."}, "29": {"original": "If you possess a product long-term, the software inside should be free so users", "rephrased": "When a consumer possesses a physical product for the long term, the software embedded within that device must be free to ensure users retain the freedom to modify and control the program. This stance argues that long-term possession grants users ownership rights that extend to the digital components of the hardware, necessitating that the software respects user freedom rather than restricting it through proprietary licenses. Therefore, manufacturers should be required to provide software that allows users to change the code, ensuring that ownership of the physical object translates into control over the digital functionality it contains.", "summary": "Long-term possession of hardware requires the embedded software to be free for user control."}, "30": {"original": "Software-as-a-service is too vague; instead, services should run free programs", "rephrased": "The business model of software-as-a-service is considered too vague and unhelpful for defining user rights, as it obscures who actually controls the program. Instead, service providers should be required to run free software on the customer's own hardware, ensuring that the user retains direct control over the program's execution and behavior. This approach prioritizes user autonomy over convenience, arguing that customers should not rely on a third party to execute the software if they wish to maintain true ownership and control over their digital tools.", "summary": "Services should run free software on user hardware to ensure direct user control."}, "31": {"original": "Service-as-a-software-substitute is a specific term for services running", "rephrased": "The term 'service-as-a-software-substitute' offers a precise definition for business models where a service consists of running a specific program for a user, distinguishing it from the broader and vaguer concept of software-as-a-service. Under this specific framework, users must be allowed to run the program themselves on their own devices to maintain genuine control, rather than relying on a provider to execute the code remotely. This distinction is crucial because running a non-free program or having a third party execute the code inherently denies the user the freedom to understand and control what the software is doing.", "summary": "Services running programs for users must allow users to run the programs themselves."}}
